chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Amr ibn Saeed, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked about the Muslim man who dies during a journey and there is no Muslim man with him, and with him are Christian men, and with him are his paternal aunt and his maternal aunt, both Muslim. How should his washing be dealt with? He (peace be upon him) said: 'His paternal aunt and his maternal aunt should wash him in his shirt, and the Christians should not go near him.'

And about the woman who dies during the journey and there is no Muslim woman with her, and with her are Christian women, and her paternal uncle and her maternal uncle, both Muslims. He (peace be upon him) said: 'They should wash her, and the Christian woman should not go near her, just as the Muslim woman would wash her, except that there is a shirt upon her, so the water is poured from above the shirt.'

I said, 'If a Muslim man dies and there is no Muslim man with him nor a Muslim woman from his relatives, and with him are Christian men and Muslim women, with no kinship between him and them.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The Christian man washes himself, then he washes him, for there is desperation.'

And about the Muslim woman who dies and there is no Muslim woman with her nor a Muslim man from her relatives, and with her is a Christian woman and Muslim men, with no kinship between her and them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The Christian woman washes herself, then she washes her.'

And about the Christian man who is on a journey and he is with the Muslims, and he dies. He (peace be upon him) said: 'A Muslim should not wash him, nor is there prestige, nor should he bury him, nor stand upon his grave.'

key_terms.قَمِيص: Shirt (used as a barrier during washing)

ai.seo_question: How is a Muslim's body washed if no same-gender Muslim relative is available during travel?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the jurisprudential hierarchy for washing the deceased during travel, prioritizing same-gender Muslim relatives and, in their absence, allowing cross-gender washing while clothed to preserve modesty. It further establishes that non-Muslims may wash Muslims out of necessity (idtirar), yet a Christian man traveling with Muslims is excluded from the honor of being washed or buried by them, reflecting the Shia principle of 'not bestowing honor' (la karama) on non-Muslims in ritual contexts.
